title: Murchadh goes out with the flint-carriers
summary: Sixteen years after his mother's death, Murchadh can no longer sit in his father's hall and goes north with a train of flint-carriers bound for Cnoc àrsaidh, taking up a yoke among them without a word of who he was; it is three seasons before any man there learns whose son he has been carrying flint beside.

title: The lake still climbing on the Ros dhomhain rock
summary: Passing through Ros dhomhain on his way north, Murchadh stands before the tide-rock his mother once showed him and finds the keeper's line of cuts crept a hand's width further up the stone since his childhood, so slowly that no single year's mark can be told from the year before or after.

title: Murchadh meets Ailig Spor on the flint road
summary: On the road between Cnoc àrsaidh and the ford gathering, Murchadh comes to know Ailig Spor, a young carrier from the northern flats who tells him plainly that a yoke does not care whose back it is on; the two keep the friendship the whole of the years the road gives them.

title: The flint road worn a yard deep
summary: The track between Cnoc àrsaidh and the northern river-crossing, worn by generations of carriers before Murchadh and Ailig were born, sinks a full yard below the level of the ground on either side, so that a man walking it casts no shadow beyond its banks and a stranger cresting the rise above it mistakes it for a dry ditch dug on purpose.

title: A storm survived in the sunken road's own bank
summary: Caught two days from shelter by a late storm, Ailig thinks to have the yoke-gang dig into the sunken road's bank and roof it with the carriers' own yokes rather than risk the open ground; the gang comes through with nothing worse than cold fingers, where an older carrier swears they would otherwise have lost two or three men.

title: Ailig marries by the northern crossing
summary: Ailig Spor marries a woman of a household by the river-crossing on the flint road and raises two sons and a daughter on flint-carrying wages, all three walking the near stretches of the road themselves before they are grown; Murchadh stands godfather to the eldest.

title: The households along the road remark Murchadh's unaging face
summary: It does not escape the households of the flint road, decade upon decade, that Murchadh carries a yoke with no more sign of years on him than a carrier three seasons in shows; some later carriers will not share a fire with him for reasons they give badly, but Ailig never once asks him the plain question every other man on the circuit wants to ask.

title: Ailig gives up the road for the pit-mouth
summary: In his sixty-fourth year Ailig Spor hands his yoke to his youngest son and takes the lighter work of tallying at the Cnoc àrsaidh pit-mouth; Murchadh, who could by then claim a dozen reasons to walk the far circuits instead, finds himself always coming back through Cnoc àrsaidh at the turn of a season to sit an evening with him.

title: Ailig Spor dies
summary: Ailig Spor dies in his sleep in his sixty-eighth year, four years a keeper and not a carrier, found by his own daughter with no mark of pain on him; Murchadh, two days south with a fresh gang who scarcely know his name, walks the two days back in one and stands at the graveside with a stillness the household has not seen on him before.

title: Murchadh sets the pit-mouth's free flake as a standing custom
summary: Murchadh stays at Cnoc àrsaidh the better part of a month after Ailig's burying and tells the new keeper that the pit's first flake of any new working shall go on being given free to whoever asks, as it always had, and that he will see to it himself that the custom does not lapse.

title: The hawk carved into the lintel at Àth mhòr
summary: Walking the far eastern circuit alone, Murchadh watches a young man of Àth mhòr cut a hawk into his father's door-lintel by firelight over three evenings, wings closed and the head turned back over the shoulder; the carver says only that the shape came to him whole one night and would not leave him alone until he had cut it, and no carrier ever hears of an earlier bird cut in wood or stone anywhere on Dia-thìr.

title: Murchadh sees the wolves buried at Tobar fhiadhaich
summary: In his hundred and eighty-fifth year Murchadh comes upon a household at Tobar fhiadhaich burying a wolf on its side with its legs drawn up as in sleep; asked why, an old woman of the household says the wolf keeps its own dead on the high ground and has earned better than the ditch, a care they have never spoken of outside the household before.

title: Murchadh asks his father for the north
summary: Murchadh comes south to Dùn ìseal and asks his father for the whole northern country the flint road runs through, which he has walked, he says, more times than any man living and knows better than any man living knows it.

title: The king refuses Murchadh the north
summary: The king answers that the north is Dòmhnall's to hold, given him sixteen hundred years before and well kept since, and that a share once given is not taken back for a better claim that comes after it; Murchadh rides north again within the week without asking a second time.

title: The first grievance of Ailean's line
summary: Murchadh rides out of Dùn ìseal with a face his father's household has not seen on him before, nearer pride than the young man's face he wore going north the first time, and close under the pride, by the telling of those who marked it, the first grievance the hill ever had cause to lay at a son of Ailean's own naming.
